item.title: An Unbounded Gap Between Identification and Identifiable Elicitation: Central Moments
item.description: arXiv:2610.24009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For $n\geq2$, two expectation equations identify the mean together with the $n$th central moment. How many coordinates must a report have if a one-observation loss uniquely elicits it and the report determines that moment? We prove that $n$ coordinates are necessary and sufficient among all identifiable intermediaries. The result holds on every open convex set of positive distributions on any $n+1$ distinct real outcomes. It requires no regularity of the loss, report map, identification function, or link. Thus $\operatorname{elic}_{\mathcal I}(\mu_n)=n$ while $\operatorname{iden}(\mu_n)\leq2$, giving an unbounded gap between identifiable elicitation and indirect identification. This resolves the central-moment conjecture of Frongillo and Kash on the stated domains. The proof constructs a $C^1$ manifold of supporting coefficients from the affine fibers of a convex negative Bayes risk. Translations along that manifold force an $n$-dimensional tangent space. Standardized moments of order at least three have the same exact complexity. The bound also extends to convex distribution classes with a full-dimensional raw-moment image.
item.dc:creator: Jingyi Jia

item.title: Benign Overfitting Property of the Minimum $\ell_q$ -norm Interpolant Estimator in Regression Problem via Feature Space Decomposition
item.description: arXiv:2610.24350v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper establishes high-probability, non-asymptotic upper bounds for the population excess risk of minimum $\ell_q$-norm interpolating estimators in linear regression, valid for all $1<q<\infty$ under three scenarios: convex concentration, mild moment assumptions and log-concavity. Consequently, we derive sufficient conditions for these estimators to exhibit benign overfitting. Our analysis hinges on a Feature Space Decomposition (FSD) framework, which naturally highlights the self-regularizing properties of minimum norm interpolants as well as the role of alignment between the signal and the features for benign overfitting. From a technical perspective, our approach circumvents the traditionally used Convex Gaussian Min-max Theorem (CGMT) by instead leveraging the Dvoretzky-Milman theorem. We emphasize that the FSD method has the potential to refine standard uniform convergence approaches. Furthermore, the isomorphic Dvoretzky-Milman theorem established herein -- proven under the three scenarios mentioned above -- for the $\ell_q$-norm is of independent mathematical interest.
item.dc:creator: Rados{\l}aw Adamczak, Guillaume Lecu\'e, Zong Shang, Marta Strzelecka

item.title: Asymptotic Normality of the Hill Estimator in Linear Preferential Attachment
item.description: arXiv:2610.24413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove asymptotic normality of the Hill estimator based on the largest $k_n$ degrees in a homogeneous linear preferential attachment graph with $n$ vertices. Each new vertex sends a fixed number $m\ge1$ of edges sequentially to older vertices, with attachment weight $d+\delta$ and fixed $\delta>-m$. Let $\alpha=m/(2m+\delta)$. For every deterministic sequence $k_n\to\infty$ satisfying $\sqrt{k_n}(k_n/n)^\alpha\to0$, the estimator, centered at $\alpha$ and multiplied by $\sqrt{k_n}$, converges to a centered normal law with an explicit variance strictly smaller than $\alpha^2$. The reduction relative to the Hill variance for independent observations separates into contributions from the different degree laws at different birth times and from competition for new edges. The contribution from competition is $1/m$ times that from different birth times. Representations using Gamma and beta functions give a consistent standard error and a studentized normal limit. The proof uses martingales indexed by edge attachments and comparisons with independent pure-birth processes, while retaining the integer degrees and their ties.
item.dc:creator: Tiandong Wang

item.title: Local quadratic convergence of iterated correlation matrices: bounds and counterexamples
item.description: arXiv:2610.24592v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kruskal's unpublished manuscript on CONCOR gives a local argument for convergence of successive correlations to a prescribed two-class sign pattern. We identify a failure in its stated one-step estimate and establish a replacement bound for correlation matrices in arbitrary dimension. A geometric estimate for sign-aligned centered rows yields an explicit sufficient neighbourhood of convergence and a quadratic error bound. We construct invariant families of correlation matrices with an exact scalar recurrence in every dimension at least three. These families yield counterexamples to the original estimate in every dimension at least four. The failure persists on relatively open sets of positive-definite correlation matrices. In dimensions divisible by four, an explicitly solvable subfamily provides counterexamples arbitrarily close to the prescribed fixed point and attains the asymptotic coefficient in the new bound. Quadratic order is attained by the constructed families in every dimension at least three. These counterexamples concern the quantitative estimate, not the convergence conclusion: all the exhibited trajectories converge to their prescribed sign patterns.
item.dc:creator: Ishrak Alhajj Hassan

item.title: Minimax Slope Estimation and Support Recovery under Weak Gaussian Selection
item.description: arXiv:2610.24749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In sample selection models, identifying a regression slope does not determine how accurately it can be estimated or distinguished from zero. We establish sharp uniform limits for outcome slopes in a fixed-dimensional Gaussian/probit selection model with unknown scale and an unknown covariate density bounded above and away from zero on a cube. We prove a uniform inverse bound between slope differences and observed-law Hellinger distance, allowing every nuisance parameter to differ between the two models. A matching path lies entirely within positive-correlation nonignorable selection. On parameter classes containing a feasible weak-selection neighborhood, the minimax squared slope risk is of order $n^{-2/3}$. For each prespecified minimum-signal sequence $b_n$, uniform exact support recovery is possible if and only if $n^{1/3}b_n\to\infty$, with rules allowed to depend on that sequence. The same estimator attains uniform root-$n$ slope accuracy on $\|\gamma_s\|\le M n^{-1/3}$ for each fixed finite $M\ge0$, including the exact zero-selection-slope layer. A testing-based construction establishes statistical attainability without estimating the covariate density; computational efficiency is not asserted.
item.dc:creator: Zeen Song

item.title: Sample complexity of weak-signal latent-variable models
item.description: arXiv:2610.24770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study parametric estimation in latent-variable models in the weak-signal regime, where a small signal-strength parameter $\beta$ controls the dependence of the observations on the unknown parameter. At $\beta=0$, this dependence disappears, so all parameter values induce the same observed distribution, which we call the null law. We develop a unified framework for analyzing sample complexity in the weak-signal regime by expanding the likelihood ratio around this shared null law in powers of $\beta$. We prove that if the unknown parameter is first globally identifiable at order $r$ in this expansion, then estimation to fixed accuracy requires at least on the order of $\beta^{-2r}$ samples. We further identify a likelihood-separation stability condition that is necessary for any estimator to attain this rate and, under mild regularity conditions, sufficient for both maximum likelihood and method-of-moments estimators to attain it. We also study the regime in which the target accuracy vanishes together with the signal strength, and show that global localization and local refinement may be governed by different likelihood orders, leading to distinct statistical scales. Finally, we apply our framework to broad classes of algebraically structured latent-variable models, including additive-noise channels and exponential-family models.
item.dc:creator: Amnon Balanov, Tamir Bendory, Dan Edidin

item.title: Dimension-free comparison inequalities between $f$-divergences for Gaussian location mixtures
item.description: arXiv:2610.25070v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish dimension-free comparison inequalities between the Kullback-Leibler (KL) and $\chi^2$-divergences and the squared Hellinger distance for Gaussian location mixtures with compactly supported mixing distributions. We show that both divergences are bounded by the squared Hellinger distance up to constants depending only on the radius of the support, independently of the ambient dimension and the number of mixture components. These results resolve an open question raised by \cite{jia2023entropic} and strengthen existing comparison inequalities. Our proof relies on a Gaussian interpolation argument that relates the derivatives of these divergences to differences between posterior means.
item.dc:creator: Jeonghwan Lee, Cong Ma

item.title: Conventional Inference under Nonstationary Heavy Tailed Fractional Processes & Arrays
item.description: arXiv:2610.25237v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing regression inference methods for nonstationary heavy tailed data are largely limited to unit roots tests. Functional central limit theorems (FCLTs), which are commonly used for the asymptotic analysis of nonstationary models, are inapplicable to nonstationary data characterized by a memory parameter $d<1$ and a stability parameter $\alpha<2$. Furthermore, it is well known that inference under nonstationarity is often non-conventional, and this issue is exacerbated in the presence of heavy-tailed data. The interaction of long memory and heavy tails significantly enlarges the nonstationary region---i.e., the covariate model space---where conventional inference methods typically fail. To address these challenges, we propose a new limit theory and methods that facilitate both workable asymptotics and conventional inference in regressions involving general nonstationary heavy-tailed covariate processes. Specifically, our approach develops a limit theory for heavy-tailed weakly nonstationary processes (hereafter, HT-WNPs), which lie on the threshold of nonstationarity (cf. Duffy and Kasparis, 2021, Annals of Statistics). We demonstrate that the proposed methods---including IVX-based and related instrumental-variable procedures---facilitate conventional inference for a broad class of stationary and nonstationary heavy-tailed covariates. This class includes nearly and mildly integrated arrays, as well as nonstationary fractional processes with memory parameter $1-1/\alpha<d<2-1/\alpha$, where $\alpha\in(1,2]$. Our analysis is applicable to both parametric and kernel regression models. The finite-sample performance of the proposed methods is evaluated through a comprehensive simulation study. Additionally, we provide an empirical application to the predictability of stock returns using long-memory heavy-tailed predictors.
item.dc:creator: Ioannis Kasparis (University of Cyprus)

item.title: Efficient estimation of measures of functional dependence
item.description: arXiv:2610.25421v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Measures of functional dependence that characterize both independence and perfect dependence have attracted growing interest. Despite their appealing theoretical properties, existing rank- and graph-based estimators can suffer from substantial bias under general dependence, limiting their usefulness for statistical inference. Moreover, a systematic and practically accessible framework for mitigating such bias while achieving semiparametric efficiency remains largely unavailable. In this paper, we develop a general framework for efficient estimation of measures of functional dependence through sample-splitting and cross-fitting. Our approach enables systematic bias reduction and semiparametrically efficient inference, and thus offers a flexible and theoretically grounded alternative to existing rank- and graph-based methods.
item.dc:creator: Holger Dette, Fang Han

item.title: Optimal Priors for Betting Tests with Bounded Payoffs: An Exact Efficiency Characterization
item.description: arXiv:2610.25821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Testing by betting is a powerful framework that recasts hypothesis testing as a betting game. A popular approach uses an $F$-weighted portfolio with a predefined prior $F$. For suitable priors, this approach has recently been shown to achieve the optimal expected rejection time as the error probability goes to zero at a fixed alternative. Yet, the prior $F$ changes how the portfolio test behaves near the null. This motivates the question: Which prior should we use in testing-by-betting algorithms? We study bounded scalar payoffs and introduce an efficiency measure that allows the error probability and alternative to vary jointly. Under mild assumptions, we prove that efficiency equals a logarithmic decay index of the prior near zero. This gives a necessary and sufficient condition for optimality: Beta priors have infinite efficiency, whereas suitable Robbins-type priors attain efficiency 1. As an application, we consider testing a specified mean of a bounded random variable and describe an implementation of the portfolio algorithm with almost-linear computational complexity.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Orabona

item.title: Weak Limits of Parameter Estimation in Strongly Identifiable Mixture Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.25857v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the asymptotic behavior of global maximum likelihood estimation in finite mixtures with an unknown number of components bounded by \(k\). Although convergence rates are well understood under strong identifiability, they do not determine the limiting distribution of mixing-measure loss. Under second-order strong identifiability, we establish two geometric results that connect density asymptotics to uncertainty about the mixing measure. First, we characterize the exact attainable density tangent set, accounting for the component budget shared by nonlocal vanishing components and local splitting directions. Second, we derive a sequential first-order expansion of squared Wasserstein loss, showing that its leading transportation cost is uniquely determined by the relative-density direction. Together with a Gaussian likelihood argmax theorem, these results yield joint weak convergence of the relative-density maximum likelihood estimator and \(\sqrt n W_2^2(\widehat G_n,G_*)\). The density limit maximizes a Gaussian likelihood process over the attainable tangent set, and the induced limit of \(n^{1/4}W_2(\widehat G_n,G_*)\) is generally non-Gaussian. We establish consistency of an \(m\)-out-of-\(n\) parametric bootstrap when \(m\to\infty\) and \(m/n\to0\). Numerical studies assess the approximation and distinguish bootstrap and optimization errors; a flow-cytometry application illustrates uncertainty summaries invariant to component labeling under a working mixture model.
item.dc:creator: Dung Le, Trang Pham, Alessandro Rinaldo, Nhat Ho

item.title: Structural Identifiability in Non-Gaussian Graphical Discrete Lyapunov Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.25935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies the problem of structural identifiability for graphical discrete Lyapunov models in the non-Gaussian setting from observational data. A graphical discrete Lyapunov model associated with a graph $G$ consists of the set of stationary distributions of stable first-order vector autoregressive models whose transition matrices have sparsity patterns determined by $G$. This model has a causal interpretation as $G$ can be viewed as encoding dynamic causal relationships between random variables of interest. It has been shown that generic parameter identifiability holds for reflexive directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Structural identifiability for these models remains unstudied beyond certain restrictive cases. In this work, we prove a non-constructive structural identifiability result for reflexive DAGs in non-Gaussian graphical discrete Lyapunov models by leveraging the information contained in the entire collection of stationary cumulants. We also provide a concrete algorithm for learning reflexive directed trees from stationary cumulants of orders $\leq 5$.
item.dc:creator: Qixia Luo, Elina Robeva

item.title: Dunnett's and Tukey's procedures under mixed model covariance structures: dimensional reduction of multivariate-t integrals
item.description: arXiv:2610.26115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dunnett's test compares several treatments with one control, and Tukey's test compares every pair for independent samples with a common variance. We investigate which designs and covariances for a linear mixed model remain on the ordinary Dunnett and Tukey integrals, and in which direction the constants move when the correlation changes. It is shown that for Dunnett's procedure AR(1), the Toeplitz band, alternating ante-dependence, and the random slope have roots below the ordinary analysis-of-variance value, while heterogeneous compound symmetry and heteroscedastic groups have roots above that value. For Tukey's procedure every computed non-spherical covariance lowers the root. The second goal is the dimensional reduction of these multivariate-t integrals: a normal probability mixed over one chi-square scale. Conditioning on the latent variables shared by the contrasts replaces that probability by a product of univariate normals, and the integral has the dimension of the conditioning vector plus one. Balanced compound symmetry leaves a double integral. The studentized range reduces to the Pearson-Hartley integral. The reduction stops for asymmetric overlap of four or more treatments, for four or more autoregressive or unstructured follow-up times, for pair-dependent variances or correlated disjoint pairs, and for a separate variance estimate in each group.
item.dc:creator: Dmytro Ivanchenko, Rostyslav Yamnenko

item.title: Singularities of Multidimensional Item Response Models and the Rank of the Fisher Information Matrix
item.description: arXiv:2610.26144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Statistical models in item response theory are known to be singular. This singularity manifests itself as a loss of rank in the Fisher information matrix, and the usual theories underlying AIC and BIC, which assume regularity, cannot be applied without further justification. Chen and colleagues analyzed this degeneracy and nonregular likelihood ratio tests, but their analysis does not identify all the directions that produce degeneracy or their dimensions. In this study, we analyze the entire kernel of the Fisher information matrix as a linear space for multidimensional item response models, separating the degeneracy due to rotations from that due to an over-specified latent dimension without double counting. We determine the dimension of each component and the exact rank of the information matrix, and prove a formula for computing, from the item parameters, the dimension of the degeneracy that remains after these components are removed. These results go beyond establishing the existence of singularity to identifying its causes and extent, providing a foundation for inference and model comparison in IRT.
item.dc:creator: Joe Suzuki

item.title: Inconsistency between Frequentist and Bayesian inference, approximation of improper priors and permissible priors
item.description: arXiv:2610.26422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Improper priors are widely used in objective Bayesian inference, although posterior propriety does not by itself guarantee coherence between Bayesian and frequentist assessments. We investigate this issue by approximating improper priors with proper priors and examining the convergence of the resulting posterior distributions. We introduce monotone $q$-vague convergence, which ensures pointwise Kullback-Leibler (KL) convergence of the posteriors, and study expected KL (EKL) convergence together with its total variation counterpart (ETV). Through continuous and discrete examples, we show that EKL convergence can depend on the sequence of compact sets used for approximation. In particular, convergence along one compact exhaustion need not extend to others. Our main result connects posterior approximation to inconsistency: strong inconsistency prevents both ETV and EKL convergence for any proper-prior approximation. Consequently, KL-permissible and TV permissible priors cannot be strongly inconsistent. We also introduce weak inconsistency and show that it may persist despite EKL convergence. Finally, a unified discrete framework covering the Flatland and Fraser-Monette-Ng paradoxes illustrates the distinction between these notions. In particular, ETV convergence need not imply EKL convergence, while the absence of weak inconsistency does not guarantee an EKL convergent compact approximation.
item.dc:creator: Pierre Druilhet, Erwan Saint Loubert Bi\'e

item.title: A Central Limit Theorem for Intrinsic Fr\'echet Means on Real Grassmannians
item.description: arXiv:2610.24159v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Subspace-valued data arise in dimension reduction, image-set and video recognition, and signal processing, and the Fr\'echet mean is their standard sample mean [11,9,15,23]. We establish a central limit theorem for the intrinsic sample Fr\'echet mean of i.i.d. observations on the real Grassmann manifold $\mathrm{Gr}(p,n)$, as a specialization of the general theorem of [18]. Unlike prior results which require the distribution to vanish or place negligible mass near the cut locus of the population mean, we allow a continuous, possibly positive density. To enable our results, we derive two properties of $\mathrm{Gr}(p,n)$: the first is that the union of the cut loci of all points within distance $\delta$ of the mean has volume $O(\delta)$. The second is that the Hessian of the squared distance function is integrable. We also give a smooth density on $\mathrm{Gr}(1,2)$ for which the mean is unique but the Fr\'echet Hessian vanishes.
item.dc:creator: Bipayan Banerjee, Imon Banerjee, Swagatam Das

item.title: Margin Certificates for Voting Classifiers under Mixing Dependence
item.description: arXiv:2610.24166v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Margin bounds explain why weighted votes generalize after training error vanishes, but dependent observations require concentration arguments that keep the dependence model and failure budget explicit. We study stationary mixing streams without treating dependence as a formal substitution of an "effective sample size." For a finite base class, we combine independent-block Rademacher theory for stationary $\beta$-mixing processes with a clipped margin loss to obtain an explicit uniform voting-margin certificate, whose dependence penalty is set by the number of approximately independent blocks and the coupling budget $4(\mu-1)\beta(a)$. A black-box transfer theorem shows that any i.i.d. voting-margin guarantee remains valid on a regularly spaced subsequence, with only an additive $\beta$-mixing failure probability. For votes fixed independently of a stationary finite-state reversible Markov stream, spectral concentration gives the cleaner $\sqrt{t_{rel}/n}$ rate, and a sticky-refresh construction shows this exponent is unavoidable. The constant is statistic-specific: the effective sample size is $n/\tau_{int}(g)$, with $\tau_{int}(g) \le 2t_{rel}-1$. When the dependence scale is unknown, a batch-means Student-t interval is valid up to an explicit remainder vanishing in the number of batches, with width governed by $\tau_{int}(g)$ rather than the worst-case $t_{rel}$. Experiments show: the learned-vote certificate is nonvacuous once the block count is large; a two-timescale construction gives a batch-means interval 8.1x narrower than the worst-case interval at nominal coverage (0.945); block-bootstrap and batch-means intervals undercover under strong dependence while the certificate stays valid; and on real, ordered UCI HAR sensor data the dependence-agnostic certificate reaches 0.95 coverage where naive intervals reach only 0.38.
item.dc:creator: Adria Binte Habib, Ibne Farabi Shihab

item.title: Recovering Dirichlet coefficients from even samples
item.description: arXiv:2610.24174v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this work, we determine the exact case error for recovering a Dirichlet coefficient from finitely many positive even samples with bounded additive errors. For sequences with a bounded tail and an unrestricted initial block, a polynomial estimator is minimax among all recovery maps. Its tail and noise constants admit explicit product formulas. We prove a sharp tail asymptotic on the index scale K^(3/2) and give a terminating procedure for selecting the sample count from a computable error bound.
item.dc:creator: Payam Danesh

item.title: The Geometry of Informativeness: A Bregman-Centroid Diagnostic for Partial Pooling in Multisite Trials
item.description: arXiv:2610.24398v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Two multisite trials can have the same informativeness yet differ in how reliably individual site effects can be estimated. We show that the informativeness index averages site-specific reliabilities on the logit scale and is a Bregman centroid under Bernoulli-Kullback-Leibler divergence. This explains the geometric mean of sampling variances and yields a measure of profile dispersion. Under stated conditions, we relate profile dispersion to estimation error and show when balanced allocation maximizes informativeness at fixed total enrollment. Simulations show that estimator performance depends on the reliability profile and whether the target is individual effects, ranks, or their distribution. An online credit recovery trial illustrates the diagnostics and their conditional posterior uncertainty. We recommend reporting informativeness with arithmetic mean reliability and profile dispersion. The accompanying R package poolinfo provides tools for computing the diagnostics, posterior summaries, and design calculations.
item.dc:creator: JoonHo Lee

item.title: Transformers as Adaptive Kernel Learners across Tasks for In-Context Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.24441v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transformers have emerged as a dominant architecture in modern machine learning, with in-context learning (ICL) enabling models to adapt to new tasks by conditioning on prompts, without any parameter updates. To understand the attention mechanism in transformer blocks, a growing line of theoretical work interprets ICL through the lens of classical statistical estimators. Recent works have established a connection between the attention mechanism and kernel methods, while the kernel function is usually assumed to be fixed. In practice, the query and key matrices in the attention mechanism are trained, which allows the attention mechanism to serve as an adaptive kernel method. In this work, we demonstrate that transformers can act as adaptive anisotropic kernel learners. Specifically, we study ICL for low-rank linear and multi-index nonlinear regressions, and conduct numerical simulations to show that the learned attention scores closely resemble the oracle kernels for these function classes. We then develop a general framework to analyze the generalization error of ICL by connecting transformers to the oracle kernel estimator for each function class. Our theory gives an explicit and constructive implementation of the oracle kernel estimators for these function classes using a wide and shallow transformer architecture, illustrating how the prediction is carried out by the interaction between the query token and the context tokens. Our work complements existing studies by providing numerical and theoretical evidence of how the attention mechanism adapts to anisotropic kernels in both linear and nonlinear settings.
item.dc:creator: Zhaiming Shen, Alexander Cloninger, Rongjie Lai, Wenjing Liao

item.title: The Segal-Bargmann Transform in Neural Partial Differential Equations
item.description: arXiv:2610.24497v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce a novel neural operator method based on Segal-Bargmann transform and Bargmann-Fock space for learning the solution operators of partial differential equations (PDEs). The method brings data encoding, latent-space representation, operator learning, and decoding into an unifed framework. From only finitely many observations, we establish a sup-norm reconstruction error of order $ L^{-\frac{1}{2}} $, where L is the number of complex sampling points that are decoupled with the original samplings and observations. The reconstruction error is independent of the spatial dimension and the number of original sampling points. We show that this new mesh-free Segal-Bargmann Neural Operator approach has superior performance compared to existing NO approaches like FNO, BelNet, GNOT, etc.,\ particularly in terms of pointwise control $ \sup_{x}\lvert\hat{u}_{NO} - u_{truth}\rvert $ for solutions of PDEs $ \mathcal{L}u = f $ which provides pointwise accuracy and interpretability as classical numerical solvers. We also demonstrates the reconstructions of the solution operators for higher dimensional nonlinear PDEs, which suggest that our proposed method has great potential to be applied to more challenging PDEs and to even higher spatial dimensions.
item.dc:creator: Jie Xu, Julio Castrill\'on-Cand\'as, Mark Kon, Qinxun Bai

item.title: Sharp detection and triangle likelihood limits for quadratic spherical kernel graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.24759v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study whether quadratic spherical geometry can be detected from a single observed graph. Latent positions are independent and uniform on $\mathbb S^{d-1}$; conditional on them, edges are independent with connection probability $K_{d,\beta}(t)=[1+\beta(dt^2-1)/(d-1)]/2$, where $0<|\beta|\le1$. We test this model against $G(n,1/2)$. Writing $N=(d-1)(d+2)/2$ for the degree-two harmonic multiplicity, we prove that the total variation distance tends to one when $N\ll n^{3/4}|\beta|^{3/2}$ and to zero when $N\gg n^{3/4}|\beta|^{3/2}$. At criticality, if $N\to\infty$ and $\Delta_n=\sqrt{\binom n3}\,|\beta|^3/N^2\to\Delta\in(0,\infty)$, the signed triangle captures all asymptotic testing information and the total variation distance tends to $2\Phi(\Delta/2)-1$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function. Polynomial finite-sample error bounds hold under polynomial signal scaling. The proof controls the likelihood of the dependent quadratic feature law through spectral recursions, covariance truncation and interpolation from a symmetric prior.
item.dc:creator: Ziqian Lin, Huangang Lu

item.title: A Tensor Critical Threshold in Cubic Spherical Kernel Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.24772v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We identify a strong-detection transition within the critical scale for testing cubic spherical kernel graphs against $G(n,1/2)$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent uniform points on $\mathbb S^{d-1}$. Conditional on these points, edges are independent, with connection probability \[ \frac{1+\beta Z_{3,d}(\langle X_i,X_j\rangle)}{2}. \] Here $Z_{3,d}$ is the normalized cubic zonal harmonic, with multiplicity $N_{3,d}\sim d^3/6$. Assume $n\to\infty$, $d=d_n\to\infty$, $\beta=\beta_n$ with $|\beta|\le1$, and $n\le d^A$, with $A<\infty$ fixed. Write $r_n=n\beta^2/(N_{3,d}d)$. On the critical scale $r_n\to r\in(0,\infty)$, we identify the tensor variational threshold \[ r_{\mathrm{tens}} :=\min_{0<q<1}\frac{-2\{\log(1-q)+q\}}{q^6}. \] For $0<r<r_{\mathrm{tens}}$, the log-likelihood ratio under the null admits an asymptotically Gaussian expansion in the signed triangle, and the total-variation distance converges to $2\Phi(r^{3/2}/2)-1$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function. For $r>r_{\mathrm{tens}}$, the likelihood-ratio test is strongly consistent, although the centered signed triangle still has Gaussian fluctuations. In the strict regimes $r_n\to0$ and $r_n\to\infty$, total variation tends to zero and one, respectively, even when $\beta\to0$.
item.dc:creator: Ziqian Lin, Huangang Lu

item.title: On the existence of a spectral gap for ergodic Markov chains
item.description: arXiv:2610.24808v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Characterizations are established regarding the existence of an $L^2$-spectral gap for ergodic (that is, irreducible, aperiodic, and positive) Markov chains on infinite state spaces. In particular, it is shown that the existence of an $L^2$-spectral gap is entirely determined by the behavior of the spectrum at 1. These results are applied in the analysis of a family of Markov chains constructed to show that the ergodic composition of two geometrically ergodic Markov kernels need not be geometrically ergodic.
item.dc:creator: Xavier Mak, James P. Hobert

item.title: Semi-supervised learning on singular data sets
item.description: arXiv:2610.25450v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose to model singular data clouds by subanalytic sets, and develop an approach to semi-supervised learning in this setting. It relies on a Morrey-type embedding for Sobolev spaces relative to globally subanalytic measures with possibly singular support. As an illustration, we present a greedy method based on a Monte Carlo approximation of the Sobolev norm of the candidate solutions. We report numerical experiments on point clouds sampled from real algebraic varieties, as well as a test on a classification problem based on MNIST images downsampled into $7\times7$.
item.dc:creator: Guillaume Valette

item.title: Anytime-Valid Inference in Linear Models with Clustered Outcomes: Exact Multivariate Tests and Cluster-Robust Confidence Sequences
item.description: arXiv:2610.25613v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We extend anytime-valid inference for linear models from independent scalar outcomes to units that contribute a vector of dependent outcomes. We develop a parametric and a nonparametric treatment. For the Gaussian multivariate linear model with an unstructured error covariance, we derive a closed-form Bayes factor under the right-Haar prior and a matrix-normal mixture alternative and prove that it is an exact e-value at every sample size and a test martingale in the invariant filtration. To our knowledge, this Bayes factor is new in the generality considered here: a d x q coefficient matrix, nuisance regressors and an arbitrary fixed positive-definite prior precision under the right-Haar nuisance prior. It yields sequential Hotelling and MANOVA tests with exact confidence sequences. Under a common within-cluster design, the cluster-robust Wald statistic of a pooled regression is equal to Hotelling's T^2 statistic computed from the per-cluster least-squares summaries, giving an exact Gaussian benchmark with G-1 degrees of freedom. For general clustered population least-squares projections, the corresponding sandwich statistic is an asymptotic e-process, without Gaussian, common-design or linearity assumptions. Each treatment includes growth and first-order expected stopping-time results; under stronger regularity, direct comparisons of expected log evidence identify a fixed mixture precision that maximizes expected log growth through constant order within a specified family, for a specified frequentist alternative. Applied to randomized experiments with several outcomes, the robust procedure gives asymptotically anytime-valid joint tests, confidence ellipsoids and simultaneous confidence sequences for the vector of average treatment effects from ordinary least-squares estimates and cluster-robust standard errors.
item.dc:creator: Michael Lindon

item.title: Geometric and measure-theoretic characterizations of the measure-determining property of balls in metric spaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.25698v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The question of what structural properties drive the collection of open or closed balls to uniquely determine Borel probability measures on a metric space, the ball property, has a long history in measure theory. While various sufficient conditions have been known since the 1970s, and it was shown by Preiss and Ti\v{s}er (1991) that it holds for all separable Banach spaces, Davies (1971) constructed a famous counterexample that shows it can fail on compact metric spaces. It was only recently established in van Delft (2026) that metric spaces admitting an isometric Hilbertian embedding must possess the ball property. This article provides a comprehensive structural and measure-theoretic characterization of the ball property. First, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for the ball property to fail: the collection of balls must possess sufficient combinatorial capacity, which we define as charged dyadic shattering. Second, by characterizing the ball property via $\lambda$-systems, we place classical vector space results within a unified context. Building on this to understand spaces that have the topological capacity but lack linear or geometric rigidity required to force ball-annihilating measures to zero, we relate the metric outer measure to the cylinder outer measure on countable products of Polish spaces, deriving necessary and sufficient measure-theoretic conditions for the ball property to hold. This allows us to derive a structural taxonomy on the decoupling of the metric outer measure from the cylinder outer measure. This is subsequently used to deconstruct Davies' counterexample. Finally, we introduce a minimal combinatorial generalization of the ball property, the $n$th order ball property, and show that such classes can fully recover measure determination in highly pathological constructions like Davies' counterexample.
item.dc:creator: Anne van Delft

item.title: Local data augmentation for imbalanced binary classification
item.description: arXiv:2610.26418v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Facing imbalanced binary classification, we aim at maximizing the recall while limiting the proportion of false detections in the minority class. For doing that, the present work studies the effect of several rebalancing strategies, from the uniform subsampling of the observations from the minority class, to a more involved local data augmentation scheme. To be more specific, we establish that only rebalancing class proportions cannot modify the classification performance, whereas local data augmentation is proved to have an impact on the final results. The local augmentation scheme is introduced by means of a two-step procedure. The first step randomly subsamples anchor points among the training observations. These anchor points are used in the second step, for drawing new augmentation data following an ''augmentation kernel'' to be specified. This enables us to decouple the impact of the anchor points subsampling from the one of drawing augmentation data accounting (or not) for the local geometry of the support. The experiments on synthetic data illustrate the practical performance of several strategies for subsampling anchor points combined with either a Gaussian or a diffusion-based augmentation kernel. Compared to SMOTE-like data augmentation procedures, a better performance is achieved when subsampling in the close neighborhood to the classification boundary combined with a Gaussian augmentation kernel. Furthermore in specific settings where the geometric structure of the support matters, the experimental results show that using a diffusion-based augmentation kernel outperforms the Gaussian one.
item.dc:creator: Harold Gu{\'e}neau (SAMM), Alain Celisse (LPP,MODAL), Pascal Delange

item.title: Statistical decision theory in thermodynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.26617v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce statistical decision theory in stochastic thermodynamic systems. Statistical decision theory integrates several statistical tasks, such as estimation, hypothesis testing, and classification. In this study, we consider statistical decision theory in stochastic thermodynamics, which unifies sensing, classification, and uncertainty relations. In particular, we focus on the minimax risk, the smallest achievable expected loss under the worst-case parameter choice, even with an optimal estimator. We derive lower bounds on the minimax risk using Le Cam's two-point method. The derived relationships can be used across a broader range of thermodynamic scenarios. To illustrate these relations, we study classification and distribution estimation problems in a Markov process. We demonstrate that the minimax risk provides lower bounds given by the dynamical activity in these problems. Furthermore, by examining particular dynamics, we establish that the resulting bounds simplify to uncertainty relations involving dynamical activity or entropy production.
item.dc:creator: Yoshihiko Hasegawa

item.title: Optimal Cox regression under federated differential privacy: coefficients and cumulative hazards
item.description: arXiv:2508.19640v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study two canonical problems in distributed survival analysis under federated differential privacy (FDP): estimation of cumulative hazard functions and Cox regression coefficients, allowing for heterogeneous per-server sample sizes and privacy budgets. To quantify the fundamental cost of privacy, we derive minimax lower and upper bounds that match up to poly-logarithmic factors, revealing server-level phase transitions between private and non-private regimes. Our algorithms are computationally-efficient and are based on adapting differentially private binary tree and gradient descent algorithms to handle estimating equations with dependent terms. We also study three related problems: estimation of the cumulative baseline hazard and survival functions in the Cox model under FDP, and estimation of regression coefficients under the federated label differential privacy, a relaxed privacy notion. For these problems, we develop efficient algorithms, establish theoretical guarantees and investigate minimax optimality. Numerical experiments, including a real-data application, support the theoretical findings. The proposed methods are implemented in the accompanying R package FDPCox.
item.dc:creator: Elly K. H. Hung, Yi Yu

item.title: Spacing Test for Fused Lasso
item.description: arXiv:2509.14229v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies the spacing test for the one-dimensional fused lasso. In post-selection inference for generalized lasso problems, the selective law is typically described by complicated polyhedral constraints, and the truncation limits of the resulting pivot are not available in simple closed form. We show that the one-dimensional fused lasso admits a remarkable simplification: the lower truncation boundary in the selective law coincides exactly with the next knot on the solution path. Consequently, the conservative spacing test of Tibshirani et al.~(2016), which is generally conservative in nonorthogonal settings, becomes exact for the one-dimensional fused lasso. The resulting selective $p$-value depends only on adjacent knots and has the same simple closed form as the ordinary LARS/lasso spacing statistic, without requiring additional polyhedral computations. Our analysis also gives a geometric interpretation of the fused-lasso path through a CUSUM representation of the knot values, connecting the spacing statistic with classical changepoint methods. Simulation studies confirm exact null calibration. Thus, the one-dimensional fused lasso provides a rare nontrivial example in the generalized-lasso family where exact post-selection inference is both theoretically explicit and computationally simple.
item.dc:creator: Rieko Tasaka, Joe Suzuki

item.title: Distinguishability of causal structures under latent confounding and selection
item.description: arXiv:2509.20433v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Statistical relationships in observed data can arise for several different reasons: the observed variables may be causally related, they may share a latent common cause, or there may be selection bias. Each of these scenarios can be modelled using different causal graphs. Not all such causal graphs, however, can be distinguished by experimental data. In this paper, we formulate the equivalence class of causal graphs as a novel graphical structure, the selected-marginalized directed graph (smDG). That is, we show that two directed acyclic graphs with latent and selected vertices have the same smDG if and only if they are indistinguishable, even when allowing for arbitrary interventions on the observed variables. As a substitute for the more familiar d-separation criterion for DAGs, we provide an analogous sound and complete separation criterion in smDGs for conditional independence relative to passive observations. Finally, we provide a series of sufficient conditions under which two causal structures are indistinguishable when there is only access to passive observations.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Carey, Marina Maciel Ansanelli, Elie Wolfe, Robin J. Evans

item.title: Local increment inference for time-inhomogeneous drift in Gaussian processes
item.description: arXiv:2606.05681v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study statistical inference for deterministic drifts in Gaussian process models under high-frequency observations over an expanding time horizon. Using a least squares-type contrast based on first-order increments, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality under conditions on drift accumulation and increment dependence.A key feature is that the convergence rate is determined jointly by the deterministic signal and the full covariance structure of the weighted Gaussian increments, rather than by local noise roughness alone.For power and fixed-frequency periodic drifts under Gaussian and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck covariance kernels, we derive explicit convergence rates and limiting variances, revealing distinct regimes depending on the drift structure and, for periodic drifts, the noise spectrum. These results clarify the respective roles of sampling frequency and observation horizon.
item.dc:creator: Yasutaka Shimizu

item.title: An RKHS Framework for Fixed Effects in Permanental Process Models
item.description: arXiv:2608.17908v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This short work describes an extension of the permanental process model which includes fixed effects. By starting with a prior on the fixed effects coefficients we show that, in the diffuse prior limit, the intensity function of the permanental process can be found using the representer theorem and naturally decomposed into a fixed effects term and a function which is an element of a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). We show that the limiting equivalent kernel defines an RKHS whose squared norm is exactly the limiting penalty. This allows for straightforward scientific interpretation of permanental process models and the easy incorporation of domain knowledge into the estimation process.
item.dc:creator: Matthew LeDuc

item.title: Proper scoring rules for survival times
item.description: arXiv:2609.28762v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This note presents a general form for a proper scoring rule that can be used for possibly right-censored survival data without requiring any knowledge or assumptions about the censoring process, so long as it is independent of survival time.
item.dc:creator: Philip Dawid

item.title: Optimal Community Recovery by Spectrally Initialized Variational EM in General Stochastic Block Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.04376v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove a Chernoff-exponent guarantee for the output of spectrally initialized batch variational EM after a prescribed iteration budget, without assuming global maximization of its variational objective. The iteration repeatedly estimates the entire block probability matrix and community proportions from the same sparse graph. We consider a fixed number of communities with proportions bounded away from zero and fixed, positive, distinct connectivity profiles; neither assortativity nor full rank is required. The algorithm uses simultaneous softmax updates without sample splitting or posterior thresholding. Its analysis must control the feedback between estimated parameters, soft labels and reused edges at an exponentially small risk scale. We establish a uniform one-step bound over data-dependent soft assignments whose random remainder has exponentially small expectation. Combined with an exponentially reliable regularized spectral initializer, this yields an unconditional expected misclassification rate bounded by $\exp\{-(1-o(1))J_n\}$ throughout the sparse, diverging-degree regime, where $J_n$ is the minimum nodewise Chernoff information. Matching lower bounds establish first-order logarithmic minimax optimality on local parameter spaces allowing unknown connectivity and varying community counts. The algorithm also attains the sharp first-order exact-recovery threshold. Numerical experiments illustrate refinement gains and sensitivity to initialization and imbalance.
item.dc:creator: Binghui Liu, Jiangzhou Wang, Man-Chung Yue

item.title: Low-order outcomes and clustered designs: combining design and analysis for causal inference under network interference
item.description: arXiv:2405.07979v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Variance reduction for causal inference in the presence of network interference is often achieved through either outcome modeling, typically analyzed under unit-randomized Bernoulli designs, or clustered experimental designs, typically analyzed without strong parametric assumptions. In this work, we study the intersection of these two approaches and make the following threefold contributions. First, we present an estimator of the total treatment effect (or global average treatment effect) in low-order outcome models when the data are collected under general experimental designs, generalizing previous results for Bernoulli designs. We refer to this estimator as the pseudoinverse estimator and give bounds on its bias and variance in terms of properties of the experimental design. Second, we evaluate these bounds for the case of Bernoulli graph cluster randomized (GCR) designs. Its variance scales like the smaller of the variance obtained by the estimator derived under a low-order assumption, and the variance obtained from cluster randomization, showing that combining these variance reduction strategies is preferable to using either individually. When the order of the potential outcomes model is correctly specified, our estimator is always unbiased, and under a misspecified model, we upper bound the bias by the closeness of the ground truth model to a low-order model. Third, we give empirical evidence that our variance bounds can be used to select a good clustering that minimizes the worst-case variance under a cluster randomized design from a set of candidate clusterings. Across a range of graphs and clustering algorithms, our method consistently selects clusterings that perform well on a range of response models, suggesting the practical use of our bounds.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Eichhorn, Samir Khan, Johan Ugander, Christina Lee Yu

item.title: Uniform Limit Theorems for Diffusion Means on Compact Riemannian Manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2601.02832v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Motivated by Varadhan's theorem, we study Varadhan functions and variances on compact Riemannian manifolds together with their minimizers, the diffusion means introduced in Eltzner et al. (2023). Given independent and identically distributed samples, we prove uniform laws of large numbers and uniform central limit theorems for their empirical versions. Through the small time asymptotics of gradients and Hessians of Varadhan functions, we build a strong connection to the central limit theorem for Fr\'echet means on compact Riemannian manifolds by recovering the ``non-standard'' correction term from Hotz et al. (2024).
item.dc:creator: Yueqi Cao

item.title: Coherent risk from finite models
item.description: arXiv:2602.00784v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Coherent estimators at different sample sizes need not describe the same population risk. We prove that dyadic estimators do so exactly when duplicating every scenario leaves the estimate unchanged, and recover the population dual set from the finite models. The risk of a Bernoulli loss determines the exact Wasserstein, Kolmogorov and total-variation moduli on a common bounded support. It also characterises uniform estimability, with an impossibility bound for arbitrary randomised estimators. An intrinsic floor on tail levels gives an explicit optimal Lipschitz constant and a uniform approximation defect; every deterministic vanishing floor preserves pointwise strong consistency. A nonstandard construction supplies compatible estimators at all finite sample sizes, explicit block-sum weights, and a formula for the worst-case mass created by infinitesimal tail levels. Finally, we derive uniform regret bounds for data-driven risk-averse optimisation and specialise them to stop-loss retention. Exact binomial calculations compare regularised and original estimators against the same population target.
item.dc:creator: Tomasz Kania

item.title: Finite-Sample Wasserstein Error Bounds and Concentration Inequalities for Nonlinear Stochastic Approximation
item.description: arXiv:2602.02445v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Stochastic approximation methods such as stochastic gradient descent and temporal-difference learning return either the last iterate or the Polyak--Ruppert average. We establish finite-sample Wasserstein-$p$ Gaussian approximation bounds for both outputs under a common framework combining moment bounds for the normalized iterates with quantitative Gaussian approximation of the appropriately weighted driving noise. These bounds yield convergence of admissible moments and high probability bounds with Gaussian leading terms: heavier dependence on the confidence level is confined to a correction that vanishes with the sample size. We verify the framework's conditions for nonlinear stochastic approximation with independent or Markovian observations and linear stochastic approximation with Markovian observations, with applications to stochastic gradient descent and temporal-difference learning.
item.dc:creator: Seo Taek Kong, R. Srikant

item.title: Statistical Inference and Learning for Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP)
item.description: arXiv:2602.10532v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The SHAP (short for Shapley additive explanation) framework has become an essential tool for attributing importance to variables in predictive tasks. In model-agnostic settings, SHAP uses the concept of Shapley values from cooperative game theory to fairly allocate credit to the features in a vector $X$ based on their contribution to an outcome $Y$. While the explanations offered by SHAP are local by nature, learners often need global measures of feature importance in order to improve model explainability and perform feature selection. The most common approach for converting these local explanations into global ones is to compute either the mean absolute SHAP or mean squared SHAP. However, despite their ubiquity, there do not exist approaches for performing statistical inference on these quantities. In this paper, we take a semi-parametric approach for calibrating confidence in estimates of the $p$th powers of Shapley additive explanations. We show that, by treating the SHAP curve as a nuisance function that must be estimated from data, one can reliably construct asymptotically normal estimates of the $p$th powers of SHAP. When $p \geq 2$, we show a de-biased estimator that combines U-statistics with Neyman orthogonal scores for functionals of nested regressions is asymptotically normal. When $1 \leq p < 2$ (and the hence target parameter is not twice differentiable), we construct de-biased U-statistics for a smoothed alternative. In particular, we show how to carefully tune the temperature parameter of the smoothing function in order to obtain inference for the true, unsmoothed $p$th power. We complement these results by presenting a Neyman orthogonal loss that can be used to learn the SHAP curve via empirical risk minimization and discussing excess risk guarantees for commonly used function classes.
item.dc:creator: Justin Whitehouse, Ayush Sawarni, Vasilis Syrgkanis

item.title: Tiny but uniform improvements of adaptive BH procedures via compound e-values
item.description: arXiv:2603.21424v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: After the seminal Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) procedure for controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) was proposed, dozens of papers have attempted to improve its power by adapting to the unknown proportion of nulls. We observe that most null-proportion estimates are simply compound e-values in disguise, and thus most adaptive FDR procedures can be interpreted as instances of the e-weighted BH (ep-BH) procedure of Ignatiadis, Wang, and Ramdas [2024], i.e., the BH procedure weighted by compound e-values. This lens helps us show that most existing procedures are inadmissible, and we provide uniform improvements to them. While the improvements are small in practice, they still come for free (without additional assumptions), and help unify the literature. We also use our "leave-one-out ep-BH method" to design a new method with finite-sample FDR control for the simultaneous t-test setting.
item.dc:creator: Nikolaos Ignatiadis, Ruodu Wang, Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: A Transport Geometry of Benign Overfitting
item.description: arXiv:2604.08625v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Benign overfitting, the phenomenon that interpolating noisy data can be statistically harmless, is usually characterized through effective-rank conditions on the covariance spectrum. These conditions are fragile: a perturbation of vanishing relative operator and Frobenius norm can turn a benign covariance into one whose minimum-norm interpolator has non-vanishing excess risk. We argue that the natural geometry of benign overfitting is optimal transport of the log-eigenvalues, measured in units of the sample size $n$. In log-spectral coordinates, the deterministic equivalent of the risk becomes a functional of two measures smoothed by a logistic kernel centred at the interpolation threshold $\log\kappa$. We compute its exact first variation: the threshold moves by a sensitivity-weighted average of the log-eigenvalue displacements, and the influence of each eigenvalue decays exponentially with its log-distance to the threshold. We then derive global, dimension-free stability bounds. The variance functional is $8/(27n)$-Lipschitz in the 1-Wasserstein distance between log-spectra, with a sharp constant, and is controlled more generally by a threshold-localized transport discrepancy; an analogous bound controls the bias. Consequently, any rank-$k$ update of the covariance, of arbitrary norm, changes the variance functional by at most $3k/n$, and benign overfitting survives every perturbation whose localized transport cost is $o(n)$. The results extend to ridge regression and to infinite-dimensional trace-class covariances. Matching lower bounds show that the $n$-scaling is necessary and cannot be replaced by operator norms, Frobenius norms, or dimension-normalized spectral distances. Simulations, one-step feature learning in two-layer networks, and random features of real images support the theory and delineate its limits.
item.dc:creator: Olaf Yunus Laitinen Imanov, Rana Irem Turhan, Isgandar Jafarli

item.title: Beyond the Flat-Spike: Adaptive Sparse CCA for Decaying and Unbalanced Signals
item.description: arXiv:2604.16435v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sparse Canonical Correlation Analysis (SCCA) is a fundamental statistical tool for identifying linear relationships in high-dimensional, multi-view data. While minimax theory establishes an optimal sample complexity scaling additively with the sparsity levels of the canonical vectors, computationally efficient algorithms typically suffer from a suboptimal multiplicative dependence. This computational-statistical gap is intrinsically tied to worst-case ``flat'' signal assumptions. In practice, however, multi-view signals frequently exhibit structured energy concentration, such as a power-law decay. To exploit this structural concentration and bypass the worst-case bottleneck, we propose Bilateral Spectral Energy Pursuit (Bi-SEP). Operating directly on the cross-covariance matrix, Bi-SEP is a stagewise adaptive algorithm that utilizes a proxy refinement step to dynamically track and capture cross-view signal energy. Theoretically, we establish a profile-adaptive sample complexity bound governed by the coupled energy profiles of the two views. Notably, under power-law decay models, we reveal a synergistic phase transition: the optimal linear sample complexity is attainable provided that the aggregate decay rate of the two views is sufficiently large. This result demonstrates that a highly concentrated signal in one view allows the model to accommodate a completely flat signal in its partner. Numerical experiments validate our theoretical findings, illustrating the advantages of Bi-SEP in structured, non-flat signal regimes.
item.dc:creator: Mengchu Xu, Jian Wang, Yonina C. Eldar

item.title: Cellwise and Casewise Robust Multivariate Regression with Inference
item.description: arXiv:2605.08002v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multivariate linear regression is a fundamental statistical task, but classical estimators such as ordinary least squares are highly sensitive to outliers. These may occur as casewise outliers that affect entire observations, or as outlying cells, that are individual contaminated entries in the predictor and/or response matrix. Moreover, modern datasets frequently contain missing values and are high-dimensional. To address these challenges we propose the cellwise multivariate regression (cellMR) estimator, a robust regression method that simultaneously accommodates casewise and cellwise outliers, missing data, and high dimensionality. The approach builds on a cellwise robust covariance estimator and uses ridge regularization for numerical stability. We further introduce cellBoot, a novel bootstrap-based inference procedure tailored to the cellMR framework. Relying on indirect inference, cellBoot provides asymptotically valid confidence intervals that are robust to casewise and cellwise contamination. We derive influence functions and breakdown bounds of the regression estimator and prove the asymptotic validity of the cellBoot confidence intervals. Simulations and a real genomics application illustrate the strong finite-sample performance of the proposed methods.
item.dc:creator: Fabio Centofanti, Mia Hubert, Peter J. Rousseeuw

item.title: A Decision-Theoretic View of Test-Time Training: When, How Far, and Which Directions to Adapt
item.description: arXiv:2606.15569v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Test-time training (TTT) adapts a pretrained model to each prompt via parameter updates, improving accuracy under pretraining-to-test distribution shifts. Yet, its performance often suffers from instability and sensitivity to hyperparameters such as update steps and subspace. We explain this behavior through a decision-theoretic lens, treating TTT as implicit Bayesian inference in the kernel regime. Under a Gaussian process benchmark, we show that TTT reduces prediction error when updates are spectrally matched to the prompt's signal-to-noise ratio and aligned with query-relevant eigen-directions. This perspective underpins the following results: (1) we show when fixed update steps and subspaces fail under distribution shifts, motivating adaptive strategies; (2) we prove that selecting update steps via prompt evidence admits a PAC-Bayes guarantee against overfitting; and (3) we characterize the Bayes-optimal update subspace under a linear-Gaussian correction model, yielding a scoring rule for selecting Transformer blocks and heads. Our theory helps explain the empirical instability of TTT, taking a step toward principled guidance for when, how far, and which directions to adapt.
item.dc:creator: Tomoya Wakayama

item.title: Relaxation times of non-reversible Markov processes
item.description: arXiv:2607.10801v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a systematic approach to quantify $L^2$-relaxation times for non-reversible Markov processes based on the singular value gap of the generator introduced by Chatterjee. The inverse of the singular value gap is equivalent to the relaxation time of the time-averaged transition semigroup. We show that, moreover, the inverse singular value gap of the two-point motion is equivalent to the relaxation time of the non-averaged transition semigroup, and that it provides a lower bound on the usual spectral gap of the generator. We then introduce a method for deriving lower bounds on singular value gaps for Markov processes with degenerate noise that is based on the concept of a first- and second-order collapse of the generator. It follows ideas from hypocoercivity developed in a previous series of works but is simpler and more broadly applicable. In contrast to previous results, it includes settings with non-vanishing first-order collapse, and thus applies directly to Markov chains (in continuous time), but also to diffusion processes and piecewise-deterministic Markov processes. Our approach yields sharp upper and lower bounds for several classes of examples. First applications include the proof of a conjecture by Diaconis and Miclo on a square-root speed-up for lifted random walks on abelian groups, as well as bounds on relaxation times of switching flows perturbed by noise and of non-reversible diffusion processes.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Eberle, Francis L\"orler

item.title: On the Role of Normalization in Binary Iterative Hard Thresholding for 1-bit Compressed Sensing
item.description: arXiv:2607.15530v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Binary Iterative Hard Thresholding (BIHT) is a simple, yet effective, greedy method for recovering a sparse vector from one-bit sign measurements. In its original form, BIHT performs a ``gradient-descent'' step, followed by hard thresholding. A convergence analysis of this algorithm was left open in the introductory work of Jacques, Laska, Boufounos, and Baraniuk [IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory (2013)] and has remained unresolved for over a decade, with subsequent sharp analyses studying a {\em normalized variant} instead, that additionally projects every iterate onto the unit sphere. This paper resolves that gap and characterizes when per-iteration normalization is algorithmically necessary. In the noiseless setting, we prove a universal, sample-optimal convergence theorem for the original BIHT algorithm. Specifically, with $\widetilde O(s/\epsilon)$ measurements, a deterministic, computable finite-time iterate has directional error at most $\epsilon$, simultaneously for every $s$-sparse unit vector. This matches the optimal sample dependence achieved by normalized BIHT in prior work. Under sign corruptions, we prove a sharp separation. If at most a $\tau$ fraction of signs are flipped adversarially, then BIHT, without per-iterate normalization, still reaches the robust error floor at an early iterate with a matching $\widetilde O(s/\epsilon)$ sample complexity rate as its normalized variant. This recovery, however, is not stable. We prove a scalar lower bound showing that any nontrivial corruption pattern, even one that involves only one flipped sign together with one clean sign, forces the iterates to oscillate indefinitely. Consequently, no general last-iterate convergence theorem can hold for BIHT under sign corruptions, while its normalized surrogate provably escapes this instance.
item.dc:creator: Arya Mazumdar, Prateeti Mukherjee

item.title: Characterizing Client-Independent Stationary Bias for SCAFFOLD and FedAvg in Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2608.26765v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Even when all clients optimize the same strongly convex objective, the global model parameters produced by constant-step federated learning may still have a stationary mean that differs from the minimizer. Does increasing the number of clients eliminate this bias, or can some components persist? Answering this question clarifies the limits of client averaging. To this end, we study two federated learning algorithms, \Scaf{} and matched \FedAvg{}, under full participation, a sufficiently smooth objective, and independent bounded additive gradient noise. Analyzing global stationary balance and within-round local fluctuations yields multidimensional expansions with a shared $\gamma/N$ term and explicit client-independent $\gamma^2$ coefficients, where $\gamma$ is the step size and $N$ is the client count. The \Scaf{} coefficient combines the ordinary local-update contribution found in \FedAvg{} with an additional persistent-control contribution. Although zero-sum controls cancel from the direct server increment, they change local second moments, which interact with third-order curvature to shift the stationary mean. For fixed dimension $d$ and local-step count $H$, a remainder of $O_{H,d}(\gamma^2/N+\gamma^3)$, uniform in $N$ for sufficiently small $\gamma$, identifies the second-order coefficients along arbitrary joint small-step, large-client limits after removing the shared leading term. Controlled experiments assess the predicted coefficients. In real-data analyses, finite-tail mean displacement can account for a substantial share of averaged-model parameter error, and a post-hoc comparison shows directional agreement with the derived curvature--noise structure.
item.dc:creator: Yi-Ping Tang, Guan-Ju Peng

item.title: Mutual Information Constrained Chernoff Bottleneck
item.description: arXiv:2609.37994v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The classical information bottleneck (IB) measures the relevance of a representation $U$ of $X$ to a target $Y$ by $I(U;Y)$, which does not directly characterize the error of downstream decisions. For a binary hypothesis $Y$ inferred from many separately encoded observations, the optimal error exponent is the Chernoff information between the two conditional distributions of $U$ given $Y$. We study the mutual information constrained Chernoff bottleneck, which seeks an encoder that maximizes this Chernoff information subject to a rate constraint $I(U;X) \leq R$. We show that its optimal value $C(R)$ increases strictly up to $R = H(V)$, where $V$ merges the symbols of $X$ with equal likelihood ratio, remains at the uncompressed exponent beyond, and, unlike the IB curve, need not be concave. We further show that $k+1$ outputs suffice to attain $C(R)$, where $k$ is the cardinality of $V$. We propose an alternating algorithm that updates the encoder via a generalized Blahut--Arimoto algorithm and the Chernoff parameter $s$ via a nonlinear equation, and prove that its iterates remain feasible, with nondecreasing and convergent Chernoff information. Comparing with the classical IB for $n$ samples, we show that, whenever the two objectives disagree, the IB encoder has the smaller equivocation $H(Y|U^{n})$ at $n = 1$, whereas the Chernoff bottleneck has the smaller error probability and equivocation for all large $n$. Numerical experiments confirm the theory, and on real topic-detection data from the 20 Newsgroups corpus, compressing each word to only $17\%$ of its entropy retains $90\%$ of the error exponent and nearly the accuracy of the uncompressed classifier.
item.dc:creator: Dier Tang, Guangyue Han

item.title: The Geometry of Anisotropic Dilation for Optimal Regularization
item.description: arXiv:2610.09310v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: How can structured transformations of data improve regularizer design for inverse problems? We address this question through anisotropic dilation, a direction-preserving map that rescales each point along its Euclidean ray by a positive profile on the sphere. Our analysis builds on a characterization of optimal regularizers within a broad Gibbs class, where the regularizer best matched to a distribution $P$ is determined by a direction-dependent radial summary statistic $\rho_P$. We show that anisotropic dilation acts explicitly and transitively on the space of radial summary statistics: any prescribed optimal regularizer in this class can be obtained by transforming an admissible source distribution using a single explicit profile. We characterize the resulting distributional orbits and establish conditions under which this control of regularizer geometry yields a weakly convex denoising formulation even when the original objective is not weakly convex. We also derive in closed form the profile that optimally adapts a fixed base regularizer to data. Its improvement over isotropic rescaling with respect to KL divergence is governed by a Jensen gap, for which we establish strict positivity under explicit conditions for several natural families of distributions. For jointly learning the base regularizer and anisotropic profile from samples, we establish finite-sample generalization bounds, with explicit rates when the logarithm of the profile is parameterized by linear feature models or sparse ReLU networks. Experiments on a controlled two-dimensional family and on MNIST denoising demonstrate that learning the anisotropic profile can improve reconstruction performance for both handcrafted and learned base regularizers.
item.dc:creator: Carson Newman, Oscar Leong
